benchmark: embedding throughput and query latency: CPU vs CUDA
todo: 13.1 (fills the 'GPU indexing < 1 min' check, previously unmeasured)
hardware: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3070 Laptop GPU (sm_86, 8 GB VRAM), 16 CPU threads; torch 2.11.0+cu128

corpus.source: real chunks from ai_db/ (tree-sitter chunker), not synthetic padding

target.gpu_under_60s: not measured here; the end-to-end sync test is opt-in (AI_DB_BENCH_SYNC=1) because the CPU arm costs minutes per 100 chunks. Extrapolating from 33 chunks/s, a 2000-chunk index is ~60 s on the GPU and ~2.4 h on the CPU.

reading: Throughput (141.8x) and per-query latency (10.5x) differ by an order of magnitude, and the gap is the interesting part.

A single short query cannot fill the GPU, so it pays kernel-launch and transfer overhead for a small amount of parallel work; bulk indexing can saturate it. The same hardware is 14x less useful per interactive call than per batch.
Consequence: the device matters enormously for indexing and only moderately for querying. Index on the GPU, query on either.
At 0.23 chunks/s the CPU arm is the reason a large index is impractical without a GPU: 2000 chunks is ~2.4 hours.
caveats: 0.6B model, short chunks (~500 chars). A larger model or longer sequences would shift the ratio; padding was deliberately avoided because it flatters the GPU.
Single machine, single run, no repetition. The throughput ratio is large enough that run-to-run noise is not material; the query-latency ratio is smaller and would benefit from more samples.
Absolute CPU numbers depend on core count and BLAS threading.
reproduce: uv run pytest tests/test_bench_gpu.py -m bench -q -s   (skips without CUDA or a cached model)
